clue.text: For an NCO such punishment may well involve stripes

definitions.meaning: a non-commissioned officer, such as the rank between lance and sergeant

definitions.text: such punishment may well involve stripes
definitions.meaning: physical punishment, like caning, which leaves stripes on the body

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripes' fits both halves: an NCO's rank badge is two stripes, and a caning leaves stripes too.
explanation.definitionFit: The rank above lance-corporal is an NCO grade, and the adjective names physical punishment of the body.

clue.text: Stage one, perhaps, in the development of civilisation

definitions.text: Stage one, perhaps, in the development of civilisation

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of the words before it could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A historian labels the opening step in humanity's progress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' tells you to rearrange STAGE ONE; the whole clue then describes the early period when tools were made of flint.
explanation.definitionFit: The prehistoric era of flint tools is the first stage of human cultural development.

clue.text: He hopes to find you well

definitions.text: He hopes to find you well

parts.words: He hopes to find you well
parts.note: reads like a greeting wishing someone good health, but describes a dowser hoping to locate a water well

explanation.surface: A letter-writer opens with a polite wish for your health.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowser searches for underground water with a rod, hoping to locate a source for a well.

indicators.note: complications suggests the letters of the word beside it are tangled into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A doctor advises cutting back because of chest trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complications' signals rearranging CHESTY.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-bladed tool is used to mow grass, and as a verb it means to mow or fell.

definitions.meaning: a looking-glass, used to see your reflection
a British national tabloid newspaper, the Daily ___

explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mirror is a British tabloid newspaper; 'Glass paper' pretends to be sandpaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A looking-glass reflects images, and the Daily Mirror is a well-known British tabloid.

definitions.meaning: bypasses a process by taking a quicker route
electrical faults where current takes an unintended path

explanation.walkthrough: One phrase means both taking procedural shortcuts and the electrical fault where current bypasses its proper path.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for bypassing normal procedure and also names an electrical fault.

clue.text: He takes a stand on a particular case, so to speak

definitions.text: He takes a stand on a particular case, so to speak

parts.words: He takes a stand on a particular case, so to speak
parts.note: reads like someone adopting a position on an issue, but describes a street speaker standing on a wooden crate to address passers-by

explanation.surface: A man adopts a firm position on one specific matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is a crate, 'stand' is literal, and 'so to speak' hints the man is a speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Street speakers once stood on wooden crates that held soap, hence a speaker on a makeshift platform.

definitions.meaning: liqueurs are typically served in small glasses and are sugary

explanation.walkthrough: Liqueurs come in small measures and are sugary, so the idiom for brevity describes them literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means brief and pleasant, and literally fits small, sugary drinks.

clue.text: Mother's returning on a vessel-an Oriental boat

indicators.note: returning means the word before it is read backwards, coming back the way it went

parts.note: Ma is mother, so Mother's gives MAS
a pan is a cooking vessel

explanation.surface: Mum heads back aboard a ship, and it turns out to be an Eastern craft.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'vessel-an' is a printed dash: the wordplay ends at 'vessel' and 'an Oriental boat' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat-bottomed skiff used in Chinese and South-East Asian harbours.

clue.text: Law agency involved in plot about the Queen

indicators.note: about means one piece goes round the other, enclosing it
involved suggests the letters of the word after it are entangled into a new order

parts.note: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A police body is caught up in a scheme against the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' gives TPOL from its word, and 'about' wraps that round the royal cipher. 'in' looks like a link but is taken as written at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: The international criminal police organisation helps forces across borders enforce the law.

indicators.note: form suggests the word before it takes another shape by rearranging its letters

explanation.surface: Someone describes one kind of everlasting time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' tells you to rearrange ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: An age so long it seems endless; the word is used loosely for an immeasurable stretch of time.

clue.text: I breathe fresh air in part of Spain and Portugal

parts.note: to breathe is to live or exist, which is to be

indicators.note: fresh suggests the word after it is made new by reworking its letters

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker enjoys clean air on the Iberian coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fresh' rearranges AIR into RIA; 'in part of' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the peninsula shared by the two countries, used for them together.

clue.text: Denounce former husband who may create trouble

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so the letters of the word before are stirred up

explanation.surface: Someone condemns an ex-partner who is likely to cause bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' looks like a noun for strife; it tells you to rearrange CREATE into ECRATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To curse or loathe aloud, a strong word for condemning.

clue.text: What you may say when you get the bill?

definitions.text: What you may say when you get the bill?

parts.words: What you may say when you get the bill?
parts.note: reads like a gasp of surprise at a large invoice, but a dove with a bill (a beak) makes this soft sound

explanation.surface: A diner reacts to an expensive restaurant check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coo!' is a British exclamation of surprise; 'bill' is also a bird's beak.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a mild British exclamation of surprise and the soft call of a pigeon.

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'high and mighty' suggests arrogance; each word separately defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Raised to a lofty rank or position, hence grand and powerful.

indicators.note: some means only a part of the word after it is taken, the letters lying inside it

explanation.surface: An instinctive native bird from New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes part of INTUITIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A honeyeater of New Zealand, known for its white throat tuft and varied song.

clue.text: Running easily for victory in the return game

indicators.note: in means one piece sits inside the other
return means the word for the game is read backwards

parts.note: golf is a game played with clubs

explanation.surface: A sportsman cruising to victory in the rematch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns GOLF round to FLOG. The surface suggests a rematch, but 'return' is the reversal signal and 'game' is just one sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving smoothly and without effort, like a stream or fluent prose.

clue.text: Wireless user gets a new set in ship

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a liner is a passenger ship

indicators.note: new suggests the word after it is remade with its letters in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A radio fan acquires a fresh set aboard a cruise ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges SET into STE. 'Wireless' is the old British word for a radio, so its user is someone tuning in.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who tunes in to a radio, which the British once called a wireless.

indicators.note: in speech means the word is spoken out, so we want a soundalike

parts.note: to hesitate is to pause, or wait

explanation.surface: A speaker paused while talking, being impaired.
explanation.walkthrough: In horse racing, a handicapped horse carries extra weights.
explanation.definitionFit: A racehorse given a handicap carries extra load to even the field.

indicators.note: anagram plainly tells the solver to rearrange the letters of the words before it

explanation.surface: The conclusion of a list of clues or wordplay puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'anagram' is itself the instruction: rearrange CLUES OR.
explanation.definitionFit: A shutting down or conclusion, as of a debate or a business.

definitions.meaning: describes a patient's condition when life is in danger, at the point of crisis

explanation.walkthrough: A hospital patient in a dangerous state is said to be in a ___ condition.
explanation.definitionFit: It means fault-finding, and also at a crisis point where danger is greatest.

clue.text: It's so lethargic — prod it to move

indicators.note: to move means the letters of the words before it are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is so sluggish they need a poke to get going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to move' rearranges PROD IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Sluggish and inactive, like an animal in hibernation.

definitions.meaning: a mild British exclamation of surprise
Billy Bunter, the greedy schoolboy of British comics, leaves only the scraps of any cake

explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is a famously greedy fat schoolboy from British children's stories.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a British exclamation of dismay and the small morsels left after eating.

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters of the word after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A student is very timid about defending their dissertation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning'; it tells you to rearrange THESIS.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of timid or bashful.

definitions.meaning: in cricket, a batsman who is dismissed is no longer batting
workers who are on strike have walked away from their jobs

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a dismissed batsman is said to be this; striking workers are also said to be this.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a batsman's dismissal in cricket and workers taking industrial action.

clue.text: They're important to one's standing as a rider

definitions.text: They're important to one's standing as a rider

parts.words: They're important to one's standing as a rider
parts.note: reads like reputation in equestrian circles, but means the foot supports a horseman stands in

explanation.surface: Something matters for a horseman's reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal loops hanging from a saddle hold a rider's feet, letting them stand up while riding.

parts.note: reads like a triumphant return, but describes sound bouncing back off a surface

explanation.surface: A performer staged a triumphant return.
explanation.definitionFit: A sound that reverberated back from a wall or cliff did this.

indicators.note: reforming means forming again, so the letters of the words after it take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A regiment is reorganised and recalls a refund.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reforming' rearranges UNIT and REMEMBERS together; 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A refund paid back to cover money someone spent.
